summary: RadarRewind is an interactive web app that turns NASA-ISRO NISAR radar data into simple "what changed here?" maps for any place on Earth. Users pan to a location and the app searches NASA's live catalog for every NISAR pass over it, showing footprints, a timeline and the revisit rate. They then load radar maps from different dates, pick a "before" and an "after", and see every pixel labelled as new water, water gone, darker (flooding, ploughing, clearing) or brighter (crop growth, construction), with areas in km². A play button animates the changes over time, and clicking any spot shows its radar history with a plain-language explanation. Because NISAR's L-band radar sees through clouds, at night, and reaches down through crops and canopy, RadarRewind can track floods, farming cycles and land reclamation when optical satellites are blind. That matters to farmers, city planners and disaster responders, in Egypt's Nile Delta and everywhere else.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Earth's surface keeps changing: rivers flood, rice paddies fill and drain, desert becomes farmland, cities spread. These changes are hard to see from space because clouds, smoke and darkness block normal cameras. Radar doesn't have that problem. RadarRewind makes NISAR's radar understandable to people who have never heard of "backscatter".

The idea in one line: radar works like a flashlight bouncing off the ground. Smooth water reflects the beam away and looks dark. Rough things like crops and buildings bounce it back and look bright. Compare the same place on two dates and you can see what moved.

HOW IT WORKS

1) Find passes (live NASA data): the app queries NASA's Common Metadata Repository (CMR) for NISAR collections (L2 GCOV backscatter, L2 GUNW interferograms, L3 soil moisture) over the current map view and date range. It draws each acquisition footprint, plots a timeline of passes, estimates the typical revisit interval, reads track/frame/orbit direction from the granule name, and links to the data and quick-look images. It also writes the exact command needed to process those passes.

2) Prepare the data (Python script): logs in to NASA Earthdata with earthaccess and downloads NISAR L2 GCOV files. It reads the backscatter (HH, or VV if HH is missing) from the HDF5 grid, cuts out the area of interest, and puts every date onto one shared lat/lon grid so dates line up pixel for pixel. It joins frames from the same day, reduces speckle with a 5x5 filter, converts to decibels and writes one GeoTIFF per date, plus an optional change map and stats file.

3) See change (interactive map): the browser reads the GeoTIFFs locally and lets the user pick "before" and "after" dates or play through all dates. It classifies each pixel as new open water, water gone, darker or brighter (adjustable thresholds; default water below -18 dB, change of +/-3 dB), reports areas in km² and the percent of land that changed, and shows a radar-history chart with a one-sentence explanation for any clicked spot. There are also "water now" and "raw radar" views on a satellite or street basemap.

BENEFITS

- Works when other satellites can't: through clouds, smoke and at night, every ~12 days.

- No expertise needed: colours and plain sentences instead of decibels.

- Free and open: a static web page plus a short Python script, built on NASA open data.

- Global, with a local focus: built around Egypt's Nile Delta, but works anywhere NISAR covers.

WHO IT HELPS

Farmers and agriculture ministries tracking planting and irrigation cycles; city planners watching land reclamation and urban growth; disaster teams mapping flood extent; teachers and students learning radar remote sensing.

TOOLS

JavaScript, HTML/CSS, Leaflet, geotiff.js, NASA CMR Search API; Python with earthaccess, h5py, NumPy, rasterio, pyproj.

VALIDATION

We tested the full pipeline on GCOV-structured test files containing a known 120 km² flood. The script detected 118.7 km² of new water inside the area of interest, and the web app computed the same figure from the same files. The app also includes a clearly labelled simulated sample so anyone can learn the controls before loading real data.

LIMITATIONS AND NEXT STEPS

Some dry surfaces, such as tarmac and calm sand, also look radar-dark, and wind can roughen water; adjustable thresholds and the basemap help users judge these cases. Next: add NISAR interferograms to show ground sinking along Egypt's coast, train an ML model to name crop types from the radar history, and send alerts when a watched area changes.
